newsitem.title: USA: N.H. Gov proposes $5.6 bln budget, double cig tax.
newsitem.headline: N.H. Gov proposes $5.6 bln budget, double cig tax.

text.p: Gov. Jeanne Shaheen recommended Thursday that New Hampshire spend $5.6 billion to run its state government over the next two years, including a $50 million spending and bond package to create a statewide public school kindergarten program for the first time.
New Hampshire is the only state without mandated public kindergarten.
Shaheen proposed an immediate doubling of the state's 25-cent-a pack cigarette tax to pay for kindergarten and eliminate a $37 million deficit.
If the Legislature passes the kindergarten plan, it would be a political coup for Shaheen, a first-term Democrat in a state traditionally dominated by conservative Republican.

Like her Republican predecessors, Shaheen pledged not to impose a state sales or income tax. But those predecessors also said the cost of kindergarten was so high that the state would have to enact a broad-based sales or income tax to pay for it, she too pledged not tor impose either of those taxes.
School funding in New Hampshire is now almost exclusively dependent on local property taxes.

Shaheen proposed a two-pronged approach to kindergarten. She called for spending $20 million for operating subsidies, about $1,000 per child over the next two fiscal years that would be at least partly funded by the increase in tobacco taxes.

And issuing $30 million of general obligation bonds to fund kindergarten construction. The double approach will mean "most towns will have kindergarten in the next two years," said Paul Khrone, executive director of the New Hampshire School Boards Association.
Shaheen said the tobacco tax is also needed to erase a $37 million deficit she inherited from Merrill.

"Raising the cigarette tax is not only good fiscal policy, it is good health policy," said Shaheen. "New Hampshire has the third highest teen smoking rate in the country. We know raising the cigarette tax will deter our children from smoking."

The increase, if enacted, would keep cigarettes 35 cents a pack cheaper in New Hampshire than in neighboring Massachusetts. Merchants in the towns near the border worry if cigarette prices are too high it will drive away business.
